Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Marcus Vance was thirty-nine when the scaffolding gave way. He had been standing twenty feet from the east wall when the steel pins slid free and the structure folded inward. What stayed with him was not a sound but a series of still frames: the slow arc of his coworker’s descent, the sudden silence, the way the dust settled over the rebar. In the weeks that followed, Marcus found his mind refusing to let the moment rest. His memories of the frightening event were mostly pictures or images that arrived uninvited, freezing him mid-stride or interrupting his sleep. When the pictures returned, so did the air he had breathed that afternoon. He could sometimes smell things that he smelt when the frightening event happened—acrid dust, crushed drywall, the sharp tang of wet cement. On some mornings, he would wake and taste what he tasted during the event when the memory returned, a metallic grit that coated his tongue until he could rinse it away with black coffee. He had come to believe that his own body was a traitor, summoning those sensations without warning, as if the past were still pressing against his skin. He was certain that the world had stopped making sense. His beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, leaving him to navigate days that felt arbitrarily dangerous. What frightened him most was that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He watched the same weather fronts and construction schedules cycle through the calendar, and he was convinced that catastrophe was always just beneath the surface. Alongside this, a quiet certainty took root: he is inadequate. He replayed the sequence of events on the site, tracing his own movements, measuring his reactions, and finding them wanting. He had come to believe that if he had only acted differently, the outcome might have been different. The thought settled into his chest like a stone, heavy and immovable. Divorced for two years and living alone in a small apartment near the yard, Marcus learned to manage the weight of these thoughts without collapsing into them. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger. He swallowed the heat in his throat, smoothed his face, and answered questions with a steady nod, telling himself that frustration was a luxury he could not afford. He did not let anger replace the gambling, nor did the gambling replace the blanks. The habits simply co-existed, forming a routine that kept him functioning. He reached for the baseball cards he kept in a duffel bag beneath his bunk, wagering small amounts on horse races or late-night poker games because he gambled to distract himself or feel excitement. The sharp focus required by the cards gave him a brief window where his mind stopped cycling back to the scaffolding. When the pressure built too high, or when the visual frames threatened to surface during a shift, he would deliberately try to leave his body or blank out. He would fix his gaze on a distant crane, let his breathing slow, and wait for the edges of the room to soften until the moment passed. The job site remained his daily environment, and the work did not slow. Last Tuesday, while inspecting a newly erected beam grid on a commercial complex, Marcus had to walk past a stack of freshly cut lumber that released a cloud of fine sawdust. The scent hit him, and the visual memory of the collapse surged forward, sharp and unfiltered. He stepped back, gripped the steel column until his knuckles whitened, and forced himself to breathe through the haze until he could continue. Over the past few months, he had begun taking longer lunch breaks, avoiding the eastern quadrant of the site, and calling in sick when the foreman assigned him to high-elevation work. He told himself it was temporary, just a way to keep his head clear. But when his insurance notice arrived, and when he realized he had not placed a bet in two weeks because he could not summon the focus to watch the screen, he knew he had reached his limit. He sought help now because he is tired of carrying the silence alone. What he hopes for is simply a way to keep the pictures from stealing his days, and what he fears most is that he will never learn how to live inside a world that no longer feels entirely broken.
